_about: Small-business scam topics as issue blocks for the B2B white-label newsletters (PR #13): the employer edition and the freelancer client letter. Same schema as launch/b2b/*/issues.json, minus id, n, send_date and deliver_by, which the B2B calendar sets. Sources are public FTC pages, checked Nov 2026. No product, affiliate or Scam Decoded links; examples are made up.

blocks.topic: Fake invoices for things nobody ordered
blocks.subject: Scam Watch: the past-due invoice nobody ordered
blocks.preheader: No purchase order, no payment. One rule stops most fake bills.
blocks.headline: The bill for something your business never bought
blocks.example: "FINAL NOTICE: Invoice #44871, Search Optimization Services, $489.00. This account is 30 days past due. Pay today to avoid collections."
explain: Scammers send invoices for things like search optimization, tech support or domain services that nobody ordered. Some look like they come from a company you know. Many say "past due" or "final notice" so whoever opens the mail pays it quickly to be safe.
Some arrive by email with a link or attachment. Those are often phishing, aimed at getting into the company's accounts rather than collecting the fee.
blocks.tell: If nobody can point to the order or contract, it isn't a bill. It's a request for money.
steps: **Match every invoice** to a real order, contract or person who asked for it before it's paid.
**Follow the approval steps** your company already has, even when a notice says "final".
**Report it.** Forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org and report fake invoices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
quick_hits: **Got products you never ordered?** The FTC says you can keep unordered merchandise for free.
**Unknown vendor?** Search its name with "scam" or "complaint" before anyone pays.
blocks.job: Find out who approves invoices where you work, and what to do with a bill you don't recognize. Save that person's name in your phone.

lobby.headline: A "past due" bill nobody ordered? Don't pay it yet.
bullets: Match it to a real order.

social.caption: Scam Watch: fake invoices for SEO, tech support or domain services nobody ordered, often stamped "past due". Match every bill to a real order before it's paid. Report fakes at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
social.alt: Scam Watch: a past-due bill nobody ordered? Match it to a real order, ask who approved it, report fakes.

sources.name: FTC: Run a small business? Pay your bills, not scammers (May 2026)
FTC: Scams and your small business

blocks.topic: "Your business will be removed from Google" robocalls
blocks.subject: Scam Watch: the "removed from Google" robocall
blocks.preheader: Verifying a Google listing is free, and Google doesn't call to threaten you.
blocks.headline: "Final notice: your Google listing will be marked closed"
blocks.example: "Final notice: your Google business listing is not verified and will be marked permanently closed. Press 1 now to speak with a listing specialist."
explain: A recording says your business will disappear from Google or be marked closed. Press 1 and a salesperson charges for "verification", then sells a monthly plan to get you to the top of search results.
The FTC took action against companies running this pitch. It says they weren't connected to Google, the threats were false, and they charged $300 to $700 for verification that is free.
blocks.tell: Google doesn't call to threaten your listing, and verifying one is free.
steps: **Hang up.** Don't press 1; it only marks your number as one that answers.
**Check the listing yourself** by signing in to the Google Business Profile.
**Already paid?** Dispute the charge with the card company and cancel any monthly billing.
quick_hits: **No one can promise the top search result.** Treat that promise as a red flag.
blocks.job: If you answer the phone at work, agree with your manager on one line for these calls: "We don't buy over the phone. Please send it in writing."

lobby.headline: "Removed from Google"? Hang up.
bullets: Google doesn't call to threaten you.

social.caption: Scam Watch: robocalls say a business will be removed from Google unless it pays to "verify". The FTC says verifying a Google listing is free and Google doesn't call to threaten you. Hang up; don't press 1.
social.alt: Scam Watch: removed from Google? Hang up. Google doesn't call to threaten you. Verifying a listing is free.

sources.name: FTC: Robocallers' false threat that small businesses will be removed from Google (2018)
FTC: Scams and your small business

blocks.topic: Domain "renewal" notices that aren't from your registrar
blocks.subject: Scam Watch: the domain notice that isn't your registrar
blocks.preheader: Check the renewal date inside your real registrar account before paying.
blocks.headline: The website bill that isn't from your web company
blocks.example: "DOMAIN NAME EXPIRATION NOTICE for yourbusiness.org. Annual website address listing and search submission: $89. Failure to pay may result in loss of your online presence."
explain: Letters and emails that look like a bill from the company that runs your website address. The FTC stopped one group that sent notices like these: they looked like they came from the real registrar, sometimes used a close variant of the name, and sold a "listing" with search optimization.
The FTC says most people who paid got no domain registration at all.
blocks.tell: Your real registrar is the one whose account you sign in to. A bill from anyone else isn't a renewal.
steps: **Sign in to the real registrar account** and check the renewal date there.
**Turn on auto-renew** with that registrar, so a scary letter can't rush anyone.
**Already paid?** Call the card company or bank to dispute it, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
quick_hits: **Look at the ending:** .org on a notice for a .com business is a giveaway.
**Small print matters:** "listing" or "search submission" means it isn't your registration.
blocks.job: Ask who pays for your company's website address, and pass on one rule: domain bills only get paid inside the registrar account.

lobby.headline: A domain bill in the mail? Check the real account first.
bullets: It may not be your registrar.
Pay only inside the registrar account.

social.caption: Scam Watch: domain "expiration notices" that look like a bill from your web company but sell a "listing" instead. Check the renewal date inside your real registrar account, and turn on auto-renew.
social.alt: Scam Watch: a domain bill in the mail? Check the real registrar account first. Watch for .org vs .com.

sources.name: FTC halts domain name registration scam (2010)
FTC: Run a small business? Pay your bills, not scammers (May 2026)
